title: The wedding date is written
hookLine: Sohila's first hymn speaks of death as a wedding day already fixed, asking friends for blessing (Gauri Deepaki, ang 12)

cards: Before an old Punjabi wedding, the date is fixed and written down. Friends crowd around the bride with blessings, and in the custom the hymn draws on, a little oil is poured at the threshold.
Everyone knows the day is coming. Sikhs sing a hymn at bedtime that uses exactly this picture. And the wedding it's talking about is not the one you'd expect.

teach.b: Kirtan Sohila is the Sikh night prayer, short hymns sung before sleep. It's also sung at the end of a Sikh funeral.

teach.h: SANBAT SAAHAA — THE DATE IS SET.
teach.b: Its first hymn is by Guru Nanak, in Rag Gauri Deepaki, on Ang 12, and its central line, in the original, is this: sanbat saahaa likhiaa mil kar paavahu tel.
The year and the day are written; come together, friends, and pour the oil. Then: give me your blessings, so that I may meet my Lord. The bride is the soul.

teach.h: DEATH AS A WEDDING, NOT A THREAT.
teach.b: And the wedding day, fixed and written, is the day of death. It sounds heavy. It isn't meant to be.
The hymn doesn't threaten, and it doesn't describe punishments. It turns death into a homecoming, the day the long-waiting bride from two days ago finally goes to her beloved.
It adds that this summons comes to every house, every day, and so it asks us to remember the One who calls.

teach.h: EVERY NIGHT, A SMALL LETTING GO.
teach.b: Some readers hear why it belongs at night: sleep is a small rehearsal of letting go. You lie down not knowing, trusting the morning. At a funeral, the same words tell the family: this was not an ambush.
It was a date, written, and a wedding. And the hymn is honest about its limit: it doesn't say when anyone's day is.
Only that it's written, and that the wise way to live is to remember it gently, with friends and blessing.

how: Many Sikhs recite or sing Kirtan Sohila before sleep each night, and it is also recited when the Guru Granth Sahib is closed for the night and at the end of a Sikh funeral.

o: a night prayer sung before sleep
the oil poured at a bride's doorway
the fixed, written date of a wedding

games.q: the hymn's picture — tap the pairs.

s: Kirtan Sohila is sung only at funerals
it's the nightly bedtime prayer, and it's also sung at the end of a funeral.
Sohila's first hymn pictures death as a wedding
the date is written; friends pour the oil and bless the bride as she goes to her Lord.
the hymn says exactly when each person's day will come
it only says the date is written, and that its summons comes to every house.

games.q: you're the bride, and the date is written. what does the hymn ask of your friends?
o: gather, pour the oil, and give you their blessings.
games.why: mil kar paavahu tel: come together and pour the oil, and bless me, so that I may meet my Lord.

practice: Let yourself remember, calmly, that your days are counted, as everyone's are; not to frighten yourself, just to see today clearly.
Think of one thing you'd want to have done or said if you knew the date, a thank-you, an apology, a call, and hold it lightly. Let the breath be slow, the way it is before sleep.

wordCard.voice: Saahaa, the fixed wedding date. From Kirtan Sohila's first hymn: death pictured as the soul's wedding day, already fixed, met with friends and blessing rather than fear.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: saha, the fixed wedding date; sanbat saahaa likhiaa, the year and the day are written.

carryVoice: Your line: the date is written. Death as a homecoming, not a threat. Gently, until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 12 (Kirtan Sohila, Gauri Deepaki Mahala 1)
